FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

The competition among MSM programs is intense, with a large number of institutions offering these degrees.
Programs strive to differentiate themselves by emphasizing unique curricular components such as leadership development modules, capstone projects, or global immersion experiences, which are designed to enhance employability and prepare graduates for management roles.
The rise of digital learning technologies has also led many institutions to offer MSM programs in online or hybrid formats, further increasing their reach and intensifying competition as geographic barriers to enrollment are reduced.
To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

PROPOSAL: THE HONORS INSTITUTE Organizational Change – Creation of Honors Institute and Addition to Chapter 3 The Honors Program proposes expanding its scope and consolidating its operations under a new aegis, the Honors Institute.
The new institute contains the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – entities that already fall ad hoc under the umbrella of “Honors.” The creation of the Honors Institute will require organizational change.
It will reside in Chapter 3 of the University Manual.
The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be responsible for its oversight and report to the Provost.
The Executive Director and Assistant Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be the Director and Assistant Director of the Honors Program.
An Advisory Council will be appointed by the Executive Director of the Honors Institute to include faculty representatives from Colleges across the University, Honors student leadership, and major external stakeholders.

The Honors Institute will not figure in Chapter 8 under “Centers and Institutes” (8.90.10-8.90.40) since the Honors Institute, an academic institute, is not the type of institute that this section was intended to govern.
The Honors Program is only one entity housed under the umbrella structure of the Honors Institute.
University Manual language [8.60.10-8.65.12] remains unchanged, including: ● Program Direction and Development.
The Director of the Honors Program in collaboration with the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall be responsible for overseeing the Honors Program (8.64.10) ● “The Teaching, Advisement and Assessment Committee shall conduct periodic evaluations of the Honors Program and its separate components” [8.64.12].
Rationale for the creation of an Honors Institute In its current form, “Honors” at URI is minimally competitive with Honors education at our peer flagship institutions.

First, Honors education at URI largely does not meet national best practices and standards in terms of curriculum. (The Honors Program directors will be submitting a redesigned curriculum to the Faculty Senate soon.) Second, and more important to this proposal: The “Honors” ecosystem – the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – is minimally integrated into the larger University, which has resulted in a lack of visibility and support.
In their “External Review Report” in 2023, National Collegiate Honors Council reviewers recognized that a transformation into an honors college was not feasible due to financial constraints at URI.
To compete with honors colleges all around us, and to house a 21st-century Honors Program, they recommended establishing an Honors Institute that pulls together officially the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities.
This highly visible and fully integrated entity would operate on par with the colleges and thus enhance operational efficiency.

The reviewers stated that the creation of a formal Honors Institute will “result in significant long-term returns to the University by raising its academic profile, by attracting a portion of the large number of high-achieving students who are available in the wider area but do not choose to attend URI, and by increasing the amount of annual giving to URI.” Further still, the external reviewers affirm that the success of an Honors Institute “could have ripple effects that launch the University of Rhode Island toward the highest tier of institutions in the Northeast.” Budget The Honors Institute will keep its existing budget infrastructure.
This includes a Fund 100 base budget and external Foundation funding.
The current internal funding is sufficient for the Institute’s operations.
In the shift to an IBB model, Honors will be classified as a central service; we anticipate no decrease in levels of funding to Honors operations.

University Manual language for Chapter 3 3.60.10 The Honors Institute contains the Honors Program (see 8.60.10 - 8.65.12) and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities. 3.60.11 The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall report to the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs, and shall have primary responsibility for administering the policies and procedures of this administrative unit. 3.60.12 The Executive Director shall be a non-voting ex officio member of the Honors Program Curriculum and Advisory Committee. UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE September 2005 The Executive Committee met regularly during the summer 2005 and after consideration, the FSEC agreed to bring forward to the Faculty Senate recommendations for changes to the UNIVERSITY MANUAL regarding the establishment of a committee on the undergraduate initiative on the Providence Campus and the University.
Following are each of the recommendations with rationale.
I.PROVIDENCE CAMPUS UNDERGRADUATE INITIATIVE COMMITTEE.
Background The Faculty Senate approved the establishment of a committee to provide oversight for the new Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative, which is scheduled to begin in Fall 2006. (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/428CAC.html for the 438th Report of the Curricular Affairs Committee, Faculty Senate Bill #04-05--9).
The Executive Committee drafted a charge to and membership of the committee in consultation with the Provost and appointed the committee for 2005-06.

Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of the following new sections of the UNIVERSITY MANUAL: 5.83.10 The Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative Committee shall oversee undergraduate programs offered on the Providence Campus to students admitted under the provisions of section 8.88.10.
The committee shall provide advice and support to the Vice Provost for Urban Programs and the Vice Provost for Academic Affairs during the initial stage of the initiative.
After the establishment phase, the committee shall review the initiative every 4 years.
Specific degree programs will be reviewed every three years on a staggered basis in accordance with the University’s current review policies. 5.83.11 The committee shall be comprised of the following members: one faculty member appointed by each department which offers an

undergraduate program at the Providence Campus; three faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs from departments that do not offer undergraduate programs; and a designee of each of the following: the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice Provost for Urban Programs, the Dean of University College and Special Academic Programs and the Dean of Admissions.
Faculty members shall be appointed for three-year staggered terms.
One of the Faculty Senate’s appointees shall serve as chair. 5.83.12 The committee shall meet on a regular basis and report annually to the Faculty Senate through the Curricular Affairs Committee on the status of the overall Providence Campus initiative.
Recommendations shall be forwarded to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee for appropriate action.
II.AMENDING THE UNIVERSITY CALENDAR Background On May 9, 2005, the Faculty Senate approved a revised calendar for academic years through 2010.

Early in the summer it came to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee’s attention that the change in the official date of spring break for 2006 in the approved calendar for 2005-06 created serious confusion and uncertainty for members of the university community.
The change was from the traditional week (March 13-19, 2006), which had been published and promulgated previously, to the following week - March 20-26, 2006.
As people learned of this change in spring break scheduling, a number of problems were identified.
These problems especially affect those members of the campus who must make plans, schedules, travel arrangements, etc., at least one year in advance.
In order to avoid further confusion, the Executive Committee took the unprecedented step of acting for the Senate in accordance with section 4.3 of the Faculty Senate By-Laws and changing the spring semester calendar.
It was agreed that while such action was necessary at that time, the problems that occurred with regard to a last-minute calendar change should not happen again.
As a result, the Executive Committee proposes that, except for emergencies, it should not be possible to modify an approved calendar within 18 months of the start of the semester in question.

Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of a clarification to section 8.70.13 (change is underlined) and the addition of a new section 8.70.14 as follows: 8.70.13 Recommendations regarding rescheduling class days missed within an academic year as the result of natural calamity, work stoppage, etc. shall be the responsibility of the Academic Standards and Calendar Committee, whose proposals will be subject to the approval of the Faculty Senate. 8.70.14 With the exception of circumstances stated in 8.70.13, changes to the calendar shall not be considered within eighteen months prior to the beginning of a semester.

1 Informational Report on Changes to Administrative Portions of University Manual, Chapters 1, 2, 4 , and 7 Submitted on behalf of President Dooley January 2017 University Manual Part I Statutes and Rules for the Government of the University Chapter 1 -­‐ The Board of Education, The Council on Postsecondary Education, and the President of the University Governors for Higher Education Board of Education 1.10.10 Background.
Education Act of 1981.
On May 7, 1981, the State of Rhode Island enacted "The Education Act of 1981" establishing a Board of Governors for Higher Education.

The general General assemblyAssembly voted that public higher education in Rhode Island should be regulated by a body called , at that time, found and declared it to be in the best interest of all of our citizens "to establish a “Bboard of governors Governors for higher Higher education Education.” In 2012, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that, beginning within 2013, the Board of Governors should be replaced by a Board of Education, in charge of all of public education in Rhode Island. which shall have the duty and responsibility of: (1) formulating and implementing a master plan for higher education in the state, (2) determining fiscal priorities among and eliminating unnecessary duplication between the various public institutions of higher learning, (3) setting standards, supervising and evaluating results and promoting maximum efficiency and economy in the delivery of higher educational services in the state." (See Title 16, Gen.
Laws R.I., 1956, as amended by Chap. 59, 16-­‐59-­‐1, 1981.) 1.10.11 Composition of the Board and Quorum Requirements.

The Board of Education is to consist of seventeen (17) public members appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Rhode Island Senate.
The Chair of the Governor's Workforce Board, or designee, and the Chair of the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation, or designee, shall serve as non-­‐voting, ex-­‐officio members of the board.
The Governor shall select from the appointed members a chairperson and vice chairperson.
A quorum shall consist of nine (9) members of the board.
A majority vote of those present shall be required for action.
The Chair of the Board shall have no term and shall serve at the pleasure of the governor.
The legislature in establishing the Board of Governors for Higher Education further stated that "said board shall be protected from sudden changes in membership and reversal of policy by having staggered terms for its public members." (See Title 16, Gen.
Laws R.I., 1956, as amended by Chap. 59, 16-­‐59-­‐1, 1981.)

2 1.10.12 Chief ResponsibilityTask of the Board.
According to its webpage (http://www.ride.ri.gov/BoardofEducation/BoardMembers.aspx , accessed 1/5/17), “The Board of Education is the chief policy-­‐setting body overseeing K-­‐20 education in Rhode Island.
Through its designated powers and duties, the Board helps shape the course of public education to ensure that all of the state's students receive the best possible education.” 1.11.10 Organization and Composition.
The Board of Governors for Higher Education is composed of fifteen members: twelve public members appointed by the Governor, one of whom shall be designated as chair, a full-­‐time student in good standing at the University of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College or the Community College of Rhode island, the chair of the Board of Regents for Elementary and Secondary Education, the chair of the Senate Finance Committee or designee and the chair of the House Finance Committee or designee.
In the selection and appointment of the members of the board, the Governor "shall seek persons who best serve the entire needs of the state.

Public members shall not be appointed for more than two successive three year terms each..." The chair may be a member as long as s/he serves in that capacity. (See Gen.
Laws R.I., Chap 59, 16-­‐59-­‐1 and 16-­‐59-­‐2, 1981 and reenactments through 1993). 1.12.10 Authority.
The General Statutes of the State of Rhode Island which relate to the University of Rhode Island and the authority of the Board of Governors for Higher Education stipulate that the Board of Governors "is constituted a public corporation, empowered to sue and be sued in its own name, to have a corporate seal, and to exercise all the powers, in addition to those hereinafter specifically enumerated, usually appertaining to public corporations entrusted with control of educational institutions and functions...the Board of Governors is hereby made successor to all powers, rights, duties and privileges formerly belonging to the Board of Regents for Education pertaining to Postsecondary Education." (See Gen.
Laws R.I., Chap. 59, 16-­‐59-­‐1, 1981 and reenactments through 1993). 1.13.10 Powers and Duties.

The Board of Governors for Higher Education shall have in addition to the powers and duties cited previously additional powers and duties enumerated in Section 16-­‐59-­‐4 of the Education Act of 1981 as amended by the Appropriations Act of 1981 and further amended by reenactments through 1993. (See Appendix A for delegation of powers.) Council on Postsecondary Education 1.20.10 Background.
In June of 2014, the Board of Education voted to establish two separate sub-­‐councils, one being the Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, the other being the Council on Postsecondary Education.
The Council on Postsecondary Education is chiefly in charge of those matters relating to the University of Rhode Island for which university-­‐internal approval is not sufficient. “The Council is an independent public corporation vested with the responsibility of providing oversight for the system of public higher education in Rhode Island.
This system consists of three public institutions of higher learning, the University of Rhode Island (URI), Rhode Island

3 College (RIC), and the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI), along with the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
The Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner, which operates under the direction of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, is the administrative and research arm of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.” (https://www.riopc.edu/page/Council%20overview/) 1.20.11 Composition of the Council.
The Council on Postsecondary Education comprises eight members appointed by the Governor from the members of the Board of Education, to serve until their terms on the Board expire, and one non-­‐voting student member appointed for a two-­‐year term from one of the three public Rhode Island institutions of higher learning.
The Council’s chair shall be appointed by the Governor from one of the eight voting members of the Council.
In addition, the Chair of the Board of Education shall serve on the Council in an ex officio, non-­‐voting capacity. (see RIGL §16-­‐59-­‐2). 1.20.12 Some Chief Responsibilities of the Council.

The Council’s responsibilities include (for more details, see Rhode Island General laws § 16-­‐59-­‐1 and § 16-­‐59-­‐4): (1) It shall retain all authority formerly vested in the Board of Education regarding the employment of faculty and staff at the public higher education institutions. (2) It shall prepare and maintain a five (5) year funding plan for higher education that implements the strategic financing recommendations of the Board of Education. (3) It shall prepare with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education and to present annually to the State Budget Officer in accordance with § 35-­‐3-­‐4 a state higher education budget.

Prior to submitting the budget to the State Budget Officer as required by the budget office instructions and this subsection, the Council shall present the budget to the Board of Education for its review and approval. (4) It shall appoint and dismiss presidents of the public institutions of higher learning with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, and to establish procedures for this, and with the assistance of the Commissioner to approve or disapprove vice presidents of the public institutions of higher learning appointed by the respective presidents of the public institutions of higher learning. (5) It shall delegate to the presidents of each public higher education institution the authority and responsibility for operational and management decisions related to their institutions, consistent with the goals of the statewide strategic plan for postsecondary education, provided however that the presidents may be required to provide information or updates to the council regarding any delegated operational or management decisions.

In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-­‐ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary

4 education pursuant to § 16-­‐59-­‐4” (See RI General Law § 16-­‐32-­‐2.1).

7 Appointments for Clinical Associate Professor positions shall be for three years with possible reappointments. 7.11.25c Clinical Professor.

Non tenure-­‐track clinical faculty shall not be eligible for tenure or permanent status.
There are three Clinical Faculty ranks, Clinical Assistant Professor (see 7.11.25a), Clinical Associate Professor (see 7.11.25b), and Clinical Professor (see 7.11.25c).

For more details on non tenure track Clinical Faculty, including, for example, annual review cycles and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP. 7.11.25a Clinical Assistant Professor shall hold a terminal professional degree in the clinical field with training and experience in an area of clinical specialization.
There must be clear evidence of a high level of ability in clinical practice, training and teaching.
Initial appointments for Clinical Assistant Professor positions shall be for two years with possible extension following a review.
The second appointment cycle shall be for a period of 3 years with possible 3-­‐year extensions. 7.11.25b Clinical Associate Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of a Clinical Assistant Professor, the appointee shall have had extensive successful experience in clinical practice in a field of specialization and in working with and/or

13 directing others (such as professionals, faculty members, graduate students, fellows, and residents or interns) in clinical activities in the field.
The appointee must also have demonstrated superior clinical practice and teaching ability and accomplishments.
Appointments for Clinical Associate Professor positions shall be for three years with possible reappointments. 7.11.25c Clinical Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of a Clinical Associate Professor, the appointee shall have demonstrated a degree of excellence in clinical practice and teaching sufficient to establish an excellent regional and national reputation among colleagues.
The appointee shall also have demonstrated extraordinary professional competence and leadership.
Appointments for Clinical Professors shall be for four years with possible reappointments. 7.11.29 Non tenure-­‐track Research Faculty are employed to contribute to the research mission of the institution, have salaried appointments of more than 20 hours per week (greater than 50% FTE) that exceed or are expected to exceed one year in duration, and are supported by non-­‐general revenue funds.

Non-­‐tenure-­‐track research faculty shall not be eligible for tenure or permanent status.
There are three Research Faculty ranks: Assistant Research Professor (see 7.11.29a), Associate Research Professor (see 7.11.29b), and Research Professor (see 7.11.29c).
For more details on non tenure-­‐track Research Faculty, including annual review cycles and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP. 7.11.29a Assistant Research Professors shall have demonstrated research ability and potential for contributing to the research, scholarly, or creative mission of the institution.
Appointees should be qualified and competent to direct the work of others (such as technicians, graduate students, other research personnel).
An earned doctoral degree shall be a requirement for appointment at this rank.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐ track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual, as well as excellence in performance. 7.11.29b Associate Research Professor.

In addition to the qualifications required of the Assistant Research Professor, appointees shall have extensive successful experience in research, scholarly or creative endeavors, and the demonstrated ability to propose, develop, and manage major research projects.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual and excellence in performance. 7.11.29c Research Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of the Associate Research Professor, appointees shall have demonstrated superior accomplishments to establish an excellent reputation among national or international colleagues.
Appointees should have a record of outstanding scholarly production in research, publications, professional achievements or exhibit excellence in research leadership.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual and excellence in performance.

14 7.11.30 Non tenure-­‐track Faculty of Practice will have salaried appointments of more than 20 hours a week (greater than 50% FTE) that exceed or are expected to exceed one year in duration and are supported wholly or in part by general revenue funds. They shall not be tenured and are not eligible for permanent status. Their primary duties and responsibilities shall be teaching. Appointments to Faculty of Practice positions are reserved for accomplished or distinguished individuals who have demonstrated skills and expertise acquired in their chosen field of practice. Examples include, but are not limited to, leaders in business, engineering, science, theatre, dance, music, and art. Appointees to the position of Faculty of Practice shall hold professional masters degrees or terminal degrees in their field or shall show evidence of equivalent capabilities by virtue of experience. Faculty of Practice shall be appointed after being vetted with the department and with approval of the Dean. Appointment to the position of Faculty of Practice shall be on an annual basis for a period of up to five years maximum. For details on these positions, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP.

V. 23.09.29 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Non-Standard form for curricular changes Only to be used in cases not appropriate for Kuali A Proposal to Fully Integrate the Public Relations Program into the Department of Journalism, Creating a New Department of Journalism and Public Relations Date: 10/27/23 Proposer Name: Professor Norbert Mundorf Department: Communication Studies 1.
Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.
